Challenge & Selection:

The challenge faced by me and my team was on how to sell our newly designed smartphone

into the market as there were many other big brands and many of them were already well  established, we were plagued with many questions such as, “who would buy them?”, “what is the  best approach?”, “why would ours be considered over other brands?” and so on. Thus, we decided  to use the design tool – “Learning Launch” to test out our product and to see what the customers  want and what they disliked.

Application:

Before mass manufacturing the phone, we wanted to know what features the customers

would like and so we conducted surveys listing down features and asked if they wanted it to be  included or not. And so, we started our experiment with a prototype and we had to balance the cost  of manufacturing with the sales to make some profit. Our first prototype showed a lot of promise as  it had a lot of features that many people wanted but then we could not handle the cost it would take  to make that device on a large scale and so we went back to redesigning it and changing things that  seemed unnecessary(for example keeping a 4K screen looked good on paper but was useless as  there were not many applications that could make use of it and so we decided to bring it down to  1080p or Full HD but with a higher refresh rate which actually made difference in the feel of the  screen). Customers were mainly concerned with a good camera, decent performance, good battery  life, software updates, memory, and longevity of the device. We also compared our prototype to the  existing phones in the market and found that cell reception quality was bad for the most part and so  we decided to add better antennas for our phone. So, we made a second prototype and it advertised  it on platforms such as YouTube, Facebook, Twitter. People were quite pleased with the device and  so we decided to manufacture it. Example Reflection – Visualization

1. Challenge

In my company, I play a role akin to an internal management consultant, working between the CEO,  COO, Head of IT, Head of HR, and all of the business unit heads.  In 2014, the company was approaching  an organization restructure which would involve looking at some fundamental elements of organisation  design, including management span of control, and the number of organizational layers.  I had attended  a few senior leadership meetings leading up to this point and could tell there were a number of looming  problems, most notably that each senior executive had a slightly different view of the problem and of  the definition of spans and layers.  For example, many thought that an organizational “layer” was the  same as a job grade – ie. that if we had a grade structure from Grade 1 to Grade 8 to which each  employee was allocated, that we therefore had eight organizational layers. They did not understand the  distinction of reporting layers.

The company was on a path of business decline and this reorganization project was critical to ensuring,  in the short term, that the organization was at least “right sized” and cost effective before an upward  transformation could begin.  A major consulting firm had produced a report the year before with lots of  data, statistics and charts, but it was clear most executives had either not read it in detail, or did not  understand what it was saying.

text:
Using Storytelling as a Communication tool and a

Problem-Solver

Introduction

I would like to talk about two problem statements that I have faced – the first one taught me the  importance of storytelling as an effective tool of communication and the second, of its  importance as a problem-solver. The assignment is structured in such a way that the first  paragraph in every section talks about the first problem and the second paragraph talks about the  second one.

Challenge

The first problem I faced was years ago as a student, when I got involved with building up an  NGO. As part of the organization, we provided free tuition to the under-privileged kids from  neighboring community. The problem was that due to the financially poor conditions in which  the kids were being raised at home, they seemed utterly dis-interested in getting education. They  used to say out statements like "What are we going to achieve by doing all this hard work. We  will always work as day laborers, etc." It was heartbreaking to say the least.

The second problem I faced was years later as part of the corporate world. My team and I, we  were trying to improve the performance of a digital product (an app) that helped first-time  homebuyers make a purchase by perusing through all the relevant information regarding the  houses online. Problem which I saw was thefts in homes and offices of our citizens. On  regular basis I got to read in newspapers about the thefts in homes and offices. I prototyped small device which sends message or voice call to the customer if someone enters  in the premise of home or office. text:
Visualization

Visualizing always challenges our community of designers, coders, and developers to take on the  pressing issues of our day. Each data visualization challenge involves creators working from the same  data set to compete for unique prizes. Data visualization has changed our society considerably. These  are some of the challenges faced in today’s world

VR

Virtual reality is going to have a huge impact on the potential for data visualizations, allowing people  to interact with data in the third dimension for the first time.

AR

Augmented reality may well be the single biggest change that we are going to see regarding the use of  data visualizations.

The challenge that data visualization is going to have is that those creating them need to make sure  they are doing so in an understandable and non-obtrusive way. It creates a new dynamic, where the  data overlaid needs to be clear, concise and not distracting. It’s a fine line to balance on and a real  challenge for those who are used to creating traditional visualizations.

Development

VR and AR are likely to be interesting technologies in the future, but for the time being, we are still  going to be consuming the majority of our data through traditional 2D screens. As the number of data  visualizations increases in almost every area, the chances of yours standing out decreases too as you’re  trying to get to the top of a larger and larger pile.

Differing Levels Of Understanding

As data has spread throughout society one of the elements that has become evident is that there is a  huge variation in the levels of understanding. This could even be in a high powered business setting,  where people who are used to seeing basic excel graphs do not understand anything more complex.  The idea of interactivity within visualized data is not something they would ever feel necessary. text: Reflection – Storytelling     Challenge & Selection     Storytelling is a great tool that I use all the time. I work with vulnerable populations, developmentally  disabled individuals, senior citizens, and economically disadvantaged people. Many of these people deal  with oppression and dysfunction in every aspect of their lives, they need to be empowered and  inspiration is a path to empowerment. I spend a lot of time “opening people up” and finding ways to  inspire them to improve their circumstances. When I work with seniors, we share stories for different  reasons. Often they're lonely and are so happy to share stories of their lives with me to connect and  they find meaning in sharing these experiences as a form of teaching and/or legacy, in a sense. With my  developmentally disabled clients I share stories of my life in order to help them visualize a state of  independence, I use their feedback against the context of my story to ascertain their goals, and  sometimes we use stories to better understand their interests and thought processes. I use this  information to develop different strategies to try and find a way that works for them to gain more  independence in the areas they find lacking in their lives. In discussing policy changes with a social service agency, I was  trying to explain to them the benefits of taking a more client focused approach, among other things, and  in particular, of recognizing each person as a unique being, and addressing their individual needs first  and foremost. The agency was in the grip of a “compliance culture” and its clients were failing in this  non-empathetic, rigid structure. text:
LEARNING LAUNCH

Challenge & Selection

I’m a member at an Art Direction. This Art Direction works for an advertising agency. One fine day we had a challenge. It was raised by one of the Textile Customer. He was one of the regular customers who visits very often. He questioned us about the impact on their sales even when they increased the investment put into in various impact media. The whole team took the challenge and we decided to come up with a better solution for the company with the problem or challenges that have been raised.

Application

With my experience and studies, I tried to question back to know who were our true audience, what are their fears and objections? What are they looking for? And other doubts together with my team. So around ten to twelve clients were selected who were visiting the textile store, made them into a group and we interviewed them. They listed all the challenges. The entire team knew the challenges and let them list all the challenges without influencing their arguments or interrupting them in between.

Insight & Approach

This was one of the best experiences I had. The search for solution with the entire team working together was something I personally never experienced before. We identified major problems to the product with cross checking of the ethnographic data. And made all the necessary changes that are required and the clients were very helpful for us to sort all kinds of problems they face and the whole team with the clients worked together to come up with the best solution possible for the problems respectively.

Reflection – Visualization

Challenge & Selection

The first tool I used was the tool of Visualization, or Visual Thinking, to achieve a shared  understanding of a problem space among a diverse group of stakeholders before attempting to  identify and define possible solutions to the problem. I use this approach often with our customers,  who are government agencies working to apply technology innovations to modernize their mission  or the delivery of their services to their customer, which may be U.S. citizens, businesses, and non- citizens. I have used the technique of using a straw man visualization of a problem domain with a set  of questions or prompts for discussion to allow a diverse group of stakeholders to learn from each  other in the process of defining the scope, boundaries, key elements, and relationships between  elements to consider when identifying pain points and opportunities for improvements or solutions.

Application

I start the process by creating a straw man graphic of the problem domain. To develop the straw  man graphic, I will draw from any existing material available to understand the environment. The  existing material may be operational or procedural documents, training materials, marketing  materials, GAO or other auditing reports. If materials are not available, then I conduct informal  interviews with one-three of the stakeholders who serve as my main points of contact on the  initiative.

If appropriate to the situation, I will borrow the concept to “front-stage/back-stage” from previous

research, and discussed in David Gray’s book, “The Connected Company”. The front-stage/back- stage approach helps to reinforce the notion that every service – even an internal service – has  customers with whom the service provider interacts and internal processes that enable the  organization to provide the service. text: Mind Mapping Reflection Exercise    Challenge:     There has been a complex problem in the environment I work in South Sudan. An area  that is quite dangerous as well as hazardous due to the prevailing armed conflict among  impatient and unreasonable belligerents. The conflict has also created a significant space  for opportunistic violent crimes affecting all employees both from the local community as  well as expatriates. More concerning however, is the fact that the locals are more exposed  in their various communities/residences to the violence than the expatriates who resided  and worked in secure and protected facilities.     The effect of the violence is further felt – due to the breakdown of law and order and more  importantly due to the fact that there was very poor security/police response to support  locals screaming for help/support to a pre – established Call Centre with a response force  especially during criminal attacks targeting them. Unfortunately, the effectiveness and  efficiency of the response force was very low due to limitations in manpower, weapons,  police response force had no zeal to support calls for help simply due to the little wages  they received, residences of locals were widespread and even in non – accessible areas,  amongst a host of other issues. As such it required a broader  and more human (or user) centric approach. With a view to gathering data, the  ethnography process was used – we dug deep into understanding the needs, wishes and  behaviors of the users as well as other stakeholders; that is the locals, police, drivers,  weapon suppliers, Government civil contractors etc.     This revealed the utmost need to expand the problem and innovate the entire business  model. Tesla

Design thinking improving HR process.

Challenge & Selection:

I work on an IT company in the HR department. There is a current issue on our career model and  our performance management system. At a first glance, employees are not satisfied on their  evaluations nor their career plans. Our response rate on our performance review system has  decreased over the last years. I have heard employees talk about the system lacks objectivity, hard  to follow, and it’s not appealing to use. However, it is not yet clear what the real problem is. I  believe we need to have a deeper understanding in different aspects such as: “does the current  process fits with the needs of the organization?” Or, does the career model align with the needs of  the organization?

In order to have a clearer understanding of the problem I think Visualization is a right fit to  understand and verbalize what our main customers see or think. I’d really like to know more about  why our employees feel so demotivated to participate in our performance management  processes. Perhaps, there are other reasons we haven’t considered them yet which I’d really like  to understand. I would like to have the input of all level employees: managers, mid-managers and  individual contributors.

In the techniques of visualization, I will use a flowchart, which I think it’s intuitive and easy to  follow.  I’d like to define questions that can analyze different scenarios in order to identify what  reasons are “triggering” or causing the dissatisfaction with performance evaluations. Then, I will  group the reasons on different premises of causation, for example: “by the process”, “career  model” or “external factors”.

Design thinking for innovation by UVA DARDEN

Professor: Mari Ahmed                                    Student:  Monica Garcia

Final Assignment

1. Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

We recently started a project aimed to offer professional services for SMBs in business  management consulting, located in a little region of Spain. This entrepreneurial initiative  coincided with one of the most challenging situation that our society (well, humanity as a  whole!) has faced in decades, mainly because of its sudden and unexpected occurrence,  the Coronavirus´ pandemic.

What it was an initial business management consultancy firm aimed to support customers  to adopt tools based on Data Analytics for improving decision making process, has to be  adapted to the new reality, where most of the people and enterprises interactions became  virtualized in weeks as a consequence of the lockdown measure taken by the Spanish  government, which drove to an urge for accelerating the digital transformation for all sort  of business, from the smaller to corporations.

All changes caused by the pandemic have seriously impacted the survival of most SMBs  here in Spain in a way that shakes their essence, so now their priority is to rethink their  purpose and business model, set new strategic goals, and redesign their organization  leveraged on the right mix of people, processes, and technologies. To overcome this  challenge, SMBs leader has very important support from the European Union Commission  who developed a recovery plan to fund those sorts of initiatives, which is a huge  opportunity for SMBs leaders to accomplish their recovery.

So the funds would not be a problem, but the perception by the SMBs´ owners that this is  kind of impossible task to accomplish, too much uncertainty, many new concepts to  internalize, super-fast changes in the environment. It seems that they would need to  quickly develop new skills to adapt to the new reality.

text:
Storytelling

During the design process, storytelling is used to understand the underlying problems that  consumers face when using a product or a service, and then use this knowledge in reflective  practice to formulate the solution which is tested by the consumers. Hence, storytelling  contributes to the different stages in the design process for different purposes in each step

This stage comes early in the design process. It aims to explore the problem to build an  accurate understanding of the main issue that needs to be solved. In the problem framing  stage, the storytelling can be used in this explorative initiative. It helps the design team to  engage with the user to define the problem using a qualitative data from the consumers.

Multiple storytelling sessions can be held with the consumers who meet with the persona  characteristics. Then, the data can be collected and analysed to build a generalised idea  about the problem. The advantage of using the storytelling tool is that it helps to create  empathy with the problem as the consumers tell their stories from their own perspective  describing their pain points in the process.

While the storytelling can be used in different stages of the design process as above, it is  a suitable tool to collected personalised experiences from the consumers. It may be hard  to build a generalised data based on it because of the different nature of each consumer’s  story, but I believe this is one of the strengths of the tool. It helps us to understand the  empathic experience that the users face when using a product or a service. This unique  strength point can be valuable for the design thinking process especially when it targets  specific problems such as medical interventions or personalised use cases.

Reflection – Learning Launch

I work at my design department and my challenge is to improve the design projects in industrial  design within the department in order to increase sales for clints and to spend designs budgets  on the right campaigns. The project scope includes the design department composed of 11  employees, as well as the larger design department and engineer’s department, with whom we  work closely. The project is limited to internal resources. The project should not exceed 30  business days and the solution should include an even distribution of working hours amongst  the team members. We will focus on trying to uncover what our team members, as well as key  stakeholders within the larger design department and engineer’s department, consider to be  ineffective or problematic with regard to the workflow. Our team has already gone through  several design thinking tools, so we are ready to try the learning launch tool. Broadly speaking,  the learning launch is an experiment meant to quickly test an idea and prototype. For our first  learning launch, we focused on the structure of our design tasks. In particular, we wanted to see  if we could structure our tasks, projects, and processes to adapt the methods of Scrum project  management for our work in an effort to become more agile. This tested our assumption that  the structure and execution were the main causes of our workflow challenge. Our team went  through a three-day training with a design project management coach. text:
Applying the Mind Mapping tool early in within the product development process

The Challenge

I am a member of the R&D team at a company which develops products marketed to healthcare  practitioners. R&D and marketing form a cross-functional ‘Core Team’ charged with developing and  launching new products. Very often we identify a novel solution and fit that into a perceived need,  without adequately spending time in the ‘What Is’ phase to truly understand whether this solution will  provide true and new value. The Core Team does come together to hone the product message  however this happens too late, with the best collaboration happening close to the launch when the  product has already been developed, and when marketing and educational materials are being  developed. The company has had many successful launches, but has also launched many products  which had the ingredients for a success which was never fully realized. Time and again, ‘not having the  story right’, is considered the reason that these launches were not as successful as possible. Our  organization is new to Design Thinking, and there is a lot of enthusiasm and openness for its  application within our product development process.

Tool Selection

I chose the Mind Mapping tool for this challenge. I found the video by Anna Moreno particularly helpful  for planning (https://www.coursera.org/learn/uva-darden-design-thinking-innovation/lecture/lsFRa/mind- mapping-tool). As Moreno states in her video, Mind Mapping is “Looking for patterns and  insights in the large quantity of data you collected during the exploration of What Is. The goal is to  establish criteria for the What If idea generation phase, which comes next. This is a pivotal point in the  design thinking process.”

text: Reflection paper – Visualization tool    Challenge and Selection    I chose to use the Visualization tool in order to solve one of my challenges. It was a great  exercise because it helped me and my team to understand very well the problem we try  to solve. Drawing all the ideas we came up with it helped us to define and to understand  what we are talking about. I noticed the fact that all the words we use have diffrent  meanings, but when we draw what we have in mind it is better because there is no room  for interpretations.     Application    In the beginning of the process we tried to define what the problem is. Our purpose was  to come up with a creative idea – an out of the box idea. So what we have done is a  visual brainstorming. I asked my team members to draw how many ideas they have on  small papers. In this way we understood very well our ideas and we have been more  creative.     Insight and Approach  The main take aways we took from this exercise are:  First of all, we were more creative. Seeing what my colleagues drawn helped me to come  up with new ideas.  Second of all, it helped us to understand each other’s ideas and we started to build on  the others ideas.     As a next step and aspect I will change for the next time is to ask from my team mates  for more ideas and more drawings.

text:
Reflection – Storytelling tool

STORYTELLING FOR SPARKING ATTENTION AND NECESSITY

Challenge and Selection

I am a content creator on YouTube and I make videos on living a more  intentional life. I had ceated more than 15 videos, which the people enjoyed  and appreciated. However, I faced a huge challenge of increasing the average  view duration of my videos. People were watching my videos, but they left it in  between. It was not so easy for me to find out the reason. I tried to improve  content, the shoot, B rolls, animations and many such aspects. I felt that the  content was attractive/ interesting enough to hold their attention, it was  relevant, useful and yet not intriguing viewers. I constantly watched popular  You tubers and realized they had a story to share. The major problem with my  videos was that they were solving a problem without identifying a problem/  cause. The content might have seemed random to viewers, because they  couldn’t connect to it. Story telling as a part of my video, hence helped me  identify a gap and my content as a probable answer to fill in the gap. The story  helped, as it gave people, something to make an emotional connect with.

Application

One of my most successful attempts at using storytelling in my videos was in a  video on the Pomodoro Technique. This technique is a tool to beat  procrastination. However, just stating this would not have helped in  understanding the same.

So, I used a story to connect with the audience and convey the usefulness of  the technique. I narrated how all of us have sometime or the other in our lives  procrastinated and put off tasks for later. I also highlighted how this led to a  vicious cycle of unproductiveness. These were things that were relatable to  most, as they had faced this themselves and immediately understood how this  was a problem. text: Challenge & Selection:    As a  brand development manager in an FMCG company, one of my duty is to assess the actual  situation of the brands I am managing and improve the sales of our portfolio. In our home care  category, the penetration rate of many player was very high, and especially in the dish washing  category. In the product life cycle, we reached a maturity level where a new added value was  needed in order for us to gain more market share. In this phase, we conducted a lot of research  to see the consumers needs, and what can be done in order to improve the product experience.    Application:    Following an ethnographic research, we came up with a lot of ideas, that we believed that they  will make a breakthrough in the market. Following the “What is” and “What if” stages, we  selected ideas, and in order to be sure about them, we wanted to make the Learning Launch  design tool to be sure about them. We have selected a special design for our packaging that will  make the consumer enjoy how they will use our product.    The main idea, was to create a bottom up bottle, so the consumer can use all the liquid inside  the product.    Since we also produce conditioner products, we use the same bottle, and filled it with our  detergent, and used 50 people, which we considered our champions, and asked them to use it  and we got their detailed feedback through one to one interview, and also assessed the value  we are offering, in addition to their feedback if they are willing to use this new bottle shape.    As we know, the prototype should be cheap, and the process needs to be fast, thus to be as  effective and efficient as we can, and confirm the date to proceed with the development, or  disconfirm the data, and see if we pivot our idea or we drop it.    In addition to the new bottle shape, we also asked them their feedback regarding the  performance of our product, and if they see it as premium product versus the available  products in the market. text:
Chris Hammond – Design Thinking for Innovation – Reflection Activity: Mind Mapping

Challenge

I work in consulting, and a major retailer asked us to help them understand how they could make  their in-store environments “more digital”. They have a long-term plan to move towards stores  which are almost fully automated and wanted to understand how they could design a store which  moved in this direction. Their brief to us was to assess ‘what is’ – that is, the current in-store  experience for customers and staff, and explore how staff and customers in different countries  would want to experience stores in the future. From this, we could then define ‘what if’ – the criteria  needed to develop a prototype store, and ideas about what the experience should be like.

Selection

We’ve worked with design thinking methodologies in the past, and given our objective was to help  define ‘what if’ we opted for a version of the mind-mapping tool. However, as the project was  international, had a limited budget and was fast-turnaround, we opted not to bring customers into  the room at the end of the project (co-creation, which is how this technique is explained in the video  lectures). Instead we would capture their views through qualitative research and play this back to  stakeholders in the mind-mapping session.

Application

We started off by conducting our qualitative research in different countries. This meant going to the  stores, interviewing staff and customers, capturing pictures and video of the store environments and  also recording how long customers spent in store, where they went, and so-on. From this we created  a detailed picture of ‘what is’, which includes current customer journey maps for the highest priority  customer missions our client was interested in (e.g. buying a new product, upgrading their existing  product, and more).

Challenge

The challenge I have faced is related to the delivery of a cover  subassembly for the automotive industry which is delivered by a  leading supplier of the German automotive market. This product is  part of the Electronic throttle control (ETC), an automobile  technology which electronically connects the accelerator pedal to  the throttle, replacing a mechanical linkage. In other words there  is no mechanical linkage between the accelerator pedal and the  throttle valve with electronic throttle control. Instead, the position  of the throttle valve, which controls the amount of air coming into the engine is fully controlled by the  ETC software via the electric motor. Our supplier is asking for a price increase of 46%, due to rump  down quantities and increase production costs related to the product.

Selection

The learning launch method combined with visualization (as a form of visual thinking) have been  chosen to get closer to the root-cause of the problem and to understand to cost drivers coming from  the production. The helpful perspectives of colleagues coming from Automotive Supplier  Development to conduct Value Stream Analysis and from Expert Calculators to carry out CSA (Cost  Structure Analysis) have been integrated to widen the perspective and understanding we have from  the product and all integrated production costs. This has been in my concept the best alternative  available to build the negotiation strategy and to structure the measurements to be introduced.

Application

The first attempt to apply this method included visiting the production facilities located at the north- east region of Germany. We have previously prepared a cost break down including all relevant  knowledge we had about the material, montage and overhead costs submitted by the supplier from  the past. text:
Reflection – Peer-Graded Assignment:

Redesigning the Youth’s Perspectives on Agriculture

Challenge:

I work in the humanitarian sector at an organization that aims at reducing world hunger and promoting  food security through activities and interventions within the agriculture sector. While outreaching for  participants to one of our agriculture programs, we fell short on recruiting young participants ranging  between 18 and 23 years old. As we needed to meet our target, this was a challenge we had to overcome.  Studying the what is of the agriculture sector in our community, we realized that there are 3 main  stereotypes that might be the reasons behind the lack of interest of the youth in the agriculture sector:

1) Agriculture practitioners are all poor, uneducated and underprivileged.   2) Agriculture practitioners are just for the old.  3) Agriculture activities are physically demanding and boring.

Breaking down those attitudes brought to my attention that with most of the people interviewed and  observed, those stereotypes emerged mostly from our own representations of this sector: if I ask you to  design a marketing campaign to promote agriculture, what would be the first pitch? In my community, the  answer has always been the same: photographs of an old man sweating and cultivating the soil, as an old  woman wearing teared clothes carries a ton of seeds over her head. It is all in the images we represent this  sector through. If however, we want the youth to be interested, then we need to show them the interesting  part of story. As an agriculture practitioner myself, I have experienced how agriculture can be fun,  developmental, and a constructive hobby to a 23-year-old educated girl like me. The challenge was to  relay this image of agriculture to an audience that have long believed otherwise.

text: Challenge  Some time ago I worked in a graphic design company, and we were asked to redesign some  posters for a charity. The charity was one of the oldest and best known in the country, but  their market dominance had been challenged in recent times by competition from several  new NGOs. The executives were set in their ways; they employed the same tactics and  messaging for every marketing campaign. They wanted to stay with the ‘safe’ option - the  one which had worked for them for years - even though they were losing their core audience  to the fresh new competition. They were firm believers that the information had to be  presented in a specific way in order to honor the cause. We were tasked with coming up with  a marketing campaign which could regain strength and position within the market.    Selection  In order to speak to all audiences we decided we needed to tell a story. As expressed by  Billy Salinas in the ​Storytelling Tool​ video in Week 2 of this course, we had to create a  cause which people could easily understand and buy into. We realized we had to find the  right story, and the right way to tell it, in order to re-engage the customers and give the  charity executives the confidence to do something different. We saw that the messaging was often quite complex, dealing with hugely  emotive topics and language which was largely unaccessible. These campaigns did not  perform as well as expected on the street with customers. In fact, many customers were put  off by the complexity of the messaging. We fully immersed ourselves in the data and tried to  find the simplest ways to re-present it. Name:   Arnaldo Campos

Due to the quarantine  imposed in my country, I’m currently taking virtual classes at my university, which didn’t  have enough experience imparting online courses before. There was some kind of cubicles with tables  and whiteboards that help us study together and sketch any idea that we may have. Hence, the challenge for me  is to implement a kind of visualization using our laptops or another way to communicate  graphical ideas to understand situations.

VISUALISATION

CHALLENGE AND SELECTION   The first tool I used was the tool of Visualization, or Visual Thinking,  to achieve a shared understanding of a problem space among a diverse group of stakeholders before  attempting to identify and define possible solutions to the problem. I use this approach often with  our customers, who are government agencies working to apply technology innovations to modernize  their mission or the delivery of their services to their customer, which may be U.S. citizens,  businesses, and non-citizens.

APPLICATION   I start the process by creating a straw man graphic of the problem domain. To  develop the straw man graphic, I will draw from any existing material available to understand the  environment. The existing material may be operational or procedural documents, training materials,  marketing materials, GAO or other auditing reports. If materials are not available, then I conduct  informal interviews with one-three of the stakeholders who serve as my main points of contact on  the initiative.

If appropriate to the situation, I will borrow the concept to “front-stage/back-stage” from previous  research, and discussed in David Gray’s book, “The Connected Company”. The front-stage/back- stage approach helps to reinforce the notion that every service – even an internal service – has  customers with whom the service provider interacts and internal processes that enable the  organization to provide the service. The straw man graphic is simple, using simple shapes and icons  available in Visio or on the Internet. If the front-stage/back-stage view doesn’t work, then I will  create a different type of visual, either based on a high-level process flow with swim lanes for  different stakeholders, or another format.

REFLECTION - MIND MAPPING

1. CHALLENGE & SELECTION :

Mind mapping is an efective way of summarising lots  of information in an easy to understand way, in an or- ganised, interesting and impactful form. It helps in  converting monotonous information into a colorful  and highly organised and simplifed diagram which  simplifes things for our brain exponentially. “Mind  mapping is looking for patterns and insights in the  large quantity of data collected during the explora- tions of what is”.

Our brain is capable of thinking a lot of things at a  time, thus managing our thoughts and ideas becomes  a very difcult task. In cases/ scenarios like these, the  mind mapping tool lets us capture thoughts, ideas and  keywords, thus summarising our concepts by retaining  just the important part.

2. APPLICATION :

According to me mind mapping tool is very helpful in  things like memorising, organisation of ideas, making  presentations, brainstorming and solving of problems. Being a design student, I am going to share a personal ex- perience with all of you which will ultimately prove the im- portance of the tool ‘Mind mapping’.

it is divided into four department. Namely;

1. The preschool department which includes creche to kindergarten.

2. The lower primary department which also includes class one to class three.

3. The upper primary department made up of class four to class six.

4. The JHS department which is also made up of JHS1 and JHS3.

The population of the students in the institution is nine hundred (900).

For the past one year, we have had some challenges which is really affecting sales and

also diminishing the good name of the institution. This was as a result of pupil absenting

themselves from school and also leaving the institution. Due to the challenges, the population of

the school declined drastically. So we are going to discover the factors that brought about this

Reflection: Kneading our future

Challenge

Running an independent bakery, as with any small shop, presents a set of challenges in a world led by  chain stores. We are competing with giants who promise lower costs, longer menus and more locations.  Back when our project started, most days we felt like the shop – we – were simply surviving, working  long hours, generating little profit, and barely keeping heads above water.

The French Baker had been a family business since 1970. My parents had opened the first brick and  mortar back in France, in the small town of Albi, and moved to Alexandria, VA in 1982. The store quite  literally moved overseas with us. When my parents died in 2002, I took over the shop and, in homage to  their legacy, kept everything as it was. By 2012, we had a small set of specialties we’d stuck to for 44  years – 20 staples that drew a crowd of regulars – but that model was no longer sustainable. By 2010, a  10% profit loss was having us headed towards closure.

Selection

We needed to refresh, a new brand, an edge. As I shaped my vision for The French Baker, I opted to tell  a story. Storytelling provided an opportunity to showcase the French Baker’s identity through the  decades and reveal its essence. I wanted the team, the store, to emotionally connect with customers by  telling our family’s story in a way that clients could understand and relate to. We had lost customers – or  simply bored them to competition – because we had become just another place that makes bread. But,  really, who doesn’t love sweets? Or bread? More importantly, who isn’t emotionally connected, moved  even, by the taste of a cookie or a cake? Drawing on our customers’ connection to food, and food’s  unparalleled ability to bring people together and memories back, I knew storytelling would be my best  bet.

We will focus on trying to uncover the technical issue in the team, as well as key  stakeholders within the IT department, consider to be ineffective or problematic with regard to ATM  downtime and technicality of fixing the problem.

text:
Challenge: mind mapping

A Mind Map is a diagram for representing tasks, words, concepts, or items  linked to and arranged around a central concept or subject using a non-linear  graphical layout that allows the user to build an intuitive framework around a  central concept. A Mind Map can turn a long list of monotonous information  into a colourful, memorable and highly organized diagram that works in line  with your brain's natural way of doing things.

Selection: I have selected this amazing tools because it makes our mind to  think broader perspective. And one can think a single point in many thoughts  The Mind Map is made even more powerful by the use of all the left and right  brain-thinking tools, which enhance the clarity, structure and organization of  your thinking.

Application: All Mind Maps have some things in common. They have a  natural organizational structure that radiates from the centre and use lines,  symbols, words, colour and images according to simple, brain-friendly  concepts. Mind Mapping converts a long list of monotonous information into a  colourful, memorable and highly organized diagram that works in line with  your brain's natural way of doing things.

Insight: One simple way to understand a Mind Map is by comparing it to a  map of a city. The city centre represents the main idea; the main roads leading  from the centre represent the key thoughts in your thinking process; the  secondary roads or branches represent your secondary thoughts, and so on.  Special images or shapes can represent landmarks of interest or particularly  relevant ideas.

Approach:

The Mind Map is the external mirror of your own radiant or natural thinking  facilitated by a powerful graphic process, which provides the universal key to

unlock the dynamic potential of the brain.

Reflection – Mind Mapping

Challenge & Selection

While I was quite curious to try out the different tools of the course, the first tool  I ended up using & being a part of the execution phase was mind mapping. With a  directive to improve the team’s overall health score, we were pushed to pull all  punches to improve the experience of everyone in the team, as they work on  multiple projects across different geographies. With multiple domains & levels of  the organization at place, it was necessary to get everyone under a single room to  record the overarching pluses, negatives & changes that could be made in the  daily workings to finally increase productivity.

Application

Being part of the team, I was an active part of this exercise that saw every  member in the team, taking time off to share the positives, negatives and changes  possible in an overarching team & project management standpoint to improve  the experiences of every single member in the team. The post-its used to record  the points were then categorized to arrive at some important factors that  required our attention, with the post-its in their member communicating the  scale & the range communicated through the different perspectives provided by  each of them. business area, but also in the daily lives of millions of people. Every start-up or

established market player has an own story that helps to create a vital link to the

emotions and values of the people that are fond of using that product daily. In other

words, storytelling is something that a lot of people from different background and

occupation are feel strongly about. My own life is not an exception.  As a young

communicate with a lot of people every single day, including students and my

colleagues. After accomplishing the «Digital thinking for innovation course» I

realize that storytelling is something I really need to apply in my job in order to make

it far more interesting and appealing for students.

from my own teaching practice of unsuccessful storytelling. During the first tutorial

as an assistant of professor I was really nervous. Looking back to this moment, at

Storytelling – Augmented reality technology for the energy industry

Challenge:

I’m part of the Chief Technology Officer of a telecom company and my main goal is to understand how  emerging technologies can enable innovative ways to solve our customer’s problems. For this specific  challenge, my team and I wanted to understand how augmented reality technology can bring efficiencies  and improve operational metrics to our customers in the energy industry. We usually do this by creating  proof of concepts or validating use cases, not necessarily by creating the end product, which allow us to  understand if the idea is commercially and technologically feasible. In this case, the challenge was to  capture the real world experience of an energy field worker in a compelling way that will allow us to create  a solid use case or concept that we can validate.

Selection:

We wanted to use storytelling as a tool that will help us craft what the current reality is for an energy worker  on the field. Specifically, we wanted to know what tasks where important to them, how do they think those  tasks could be performed more efficiently, what tools they think could help them and why. We figured  storytelling will be the perfect tool to transform their challenges into a compelling story since storytelling  allows to focus on the people and their experience and serves as a way to show the problems they were  facing using a simple and clear narrative. We thought it was the perfect tool to both, synthesize all the  information we gathered and to create empathy to the stakeholders.

Reflection - Visualization

Challenge & Selection

The tool that I have used most so far, is the tool of “visualization”. At work, I have the role of the  business manager/developer and as such I need to make sure that everyone involved (stakeholders)  in the process understands what we are talking about. By that I mean: IT, Compliance, Front Office  colleagues, senior management, etc. The previously mentioned stakeholders come from different  backgrounds, fly at different altitude and use different vocabulary, and that’s the beauty of  visualization: you can usually get by without words and images/drawings usually resonate on a  almost meta-level, allowing you to achieve a common understanding much faster than with written  texts.

Application

Most recently I used the tool of “visualization” in the process of drafting a concept for a “prospecting  engine” for a company. The company already had several tools in place for that purpose, but none of  them was widely used, and the reasons for that were plentiful: not user-friendly, redundant data  entry, stand-alone tools, etc. Besides aiming to fix all those painpoints, I wanted to get to a solution  that would also allow us to leverage part of the value chain that can be sourced from third party  providers, such as “data of potentially interesting prospects”.

As mentioned above, when looking at such a venture in our company, one quickly ends up talking to  the majority of the divisions: Legal & Compliance, Sourcing, IT, Front Office but also Marketing, and  in order to pitch the idea one usually gets one shot. At this point the great strength of visualization  comes into play, and the statement we’ve heard in the online course is absolutely correct: you do not  have to be a talented graphic designer! My sketches are usually rather clumsy, but the effect is  absolutely astonishing. Images are so much easier to understand than words and leave much less  room for interpretation. Naga Raju

Design Thinking for Innovation Final Assignment

Challenges and Selection

One of the main challenges I faced as an event planner and decorator is creating a design  which suits the client’s vision and budget but does not eliminate our characteristic as a  designer. I recently faced this challenge when I was doing a wedding design project, in which  my team and I needed to communicate our design ideas and arguments clearly to the client  for them to be able to picture the design well and reach a final agreement. It was an outdoor  wedding reception, and the client wanted it to be intimate and had a rustic mood whilst still  remained on their budget. I decided to use the visualization tool to overcome this challenge  because I figured that decorating an event venue involves a lot of picturing 3D spaces and  room sequences, and this tool is the best way to avoid misconceptions when communicating  our ideas to the client.

Application

At the early step of designing after getting a short brief of the client’s vision, I composed a  design mood board which consists several wedding decoration images, color palettes and  types of flowers that we are going to use according to the big theme. This mood board really  helps us to communicate with the client regarding their design preferences before we moved  to detailing. Visualizing the design examples by real images and color palettes is proven to be  more effective rather than explaining them by words, because both I and the client were able  to state clearly which are suitable with our ideas, characteristic and budget and which are not. Mind Mapping as the tool of choice

I have chosen to apply the Mind Mapping tool. A mind map can be

used to represent a subject or an idea, structuring the information

in a map-like view. The topic is placed at center of the map (its

starting point) and then the concepts and details, are connected in

a logic, hierarchical way. For example:

Example of a mind map showing types of social networks

The example map above quickly informs the us about what the

topic is (types of social networks), what are the categories and sub-

categories (gaming, photography,…) and what are some items

within those categories (the social networks like Facebook,

Twitter, etc).

Application and insights

So after learning about the Mind Mapping tool, I started creating

maps at work and also for my MBA course. My insight was that the

tasks or assignments we execute are usually really repetition of

something already done in the past. However, although they’re

known, they are also too big or too complex for us to rely only on

our memories. Here’s where the mind mapping helps a lot.

The two below are some examples where I’m applying the mind

mapping:

• Starting a new project: using a mind map to organize

the dozens of things that a project manager has to

coordinate has greatly facilitated my work. Every project

basically contains the same items: scope (what’s in, what’s

out), timeline (dates, milestones), costs, resources

(people, equipments), risks and assumptions.

• Learning a new subject: to me, the hardest part of

learning a new subject, is visualizing how big it is and how

its concepts and details are interconnected. Creating a

mind map had a vast positive impact on my study because

I can, as I read through the pages, create the visual map

representation of the subject.

Challenge

I am a digital product designer with a strong background in product  development working at a venture builder. We are engaged in looking for  unmet customer needs/innovation potential in the markets we explore and  need to quickly validate our ﬁndings and test our assumptions in order to, in  the end, come up with solid business cases for further investment.

Of course, each exploration project requires time, people and money. None of  which can be wasted and success is rare. Thus, acceleration of the process and  minimizing the need for these scarce resources are essential. In this context,  the challenge is clear: Quickly come up with and iteratively test key  assumptions and product ideas with real customers to be able to learn and  adapt as early as possible.

Selection

We are working in a strict lean approach, as described by Eric Reis in his best- selling book „The Lean Startup“ (http://theleanstartup.com/principles) which at  its core uses a methodology called „build-measure-learn feedback loop“. Quick  iteration is the main principle. So, in terms of generating and testing ideas the  „Learning Launch“ was the preferred method.

What we test in the end is also called a „prototype“ (or in some deﬁnitions even  Minimal Viable Product) and can take many forms. Its main purpose is to create  just enough value for the user to adopt it so we can gain real-life insights and  enable us to test key assumptions without having to build the complete  product with all its features right from the beginning.

text:
If you need to brainstorm an issue, develop a new product, deliver a marketing

campaign, make a pitch for a deal or simply discuss a problem, creativity is

key. Creating a Mind Map is an excellent way of coming up with creative ways to

address the matter.

Here is a simple five-step Mind Mapping process for you to follow to create your own

brainstorming Mind Maps and boost innovation in your company.  The Quick-Fire Mind Map Burst

Begin your Mind Map by setting your central idea, theme or topic. Choose a stimulating

central image that represents the theme or topic you are addressing.

From your central idea radiate every idea that comes into your mind on that subject,

dividing them into key ideas, or main brain branches. From your main ideas/branches

add your sub ideas, or child branches. You should let the ideas flow as fast as possible.

Having to work at speed unchains your brain from habitual thinking patterns, and

encourages new ideas and innovation. Many of these new ideas may at first seem

absurd, however they often hold the key to new perspectives and the breaking of old

habits. The most innovative solutions come from the germ of an idea, and you want to

Mind Mapping - Returning to Universidad San Francisco de Quito During the Time of COVID-19

Challenge:

COVID-19 was declared a pandemic by the World Health Organization on March 11, 2020.

During that time, Universidad San Francisco de Quito students were off campus and on spring break. In the interest

of safety, Hellen Keller  Institute decided to suspend its residential program and in-class courses. Following

spring break, all Spring 2019 courses were completed remotely via Zoom and Google classroom.

On Tuesday, May 26, Hellen Keller  Institute’s President, Sean Decatur, updated students with information

regarding the 2020-2021 school year. He shared that Hellen Keller  Institute is currently planning to hold in-

person classes and continue their residential program beginning August 27th. Many adjustments

to campus life will need to be made, so as to adhere to social distancing guidelines and maintain

a healthy college campus.

In order to take a design thinking approach to this challenge, it’s important to begin with the

mind mapping tool. Mind mapping addresses the “what is” question and helps find patterns that

might allow for more creative solutions. The data accumulated can then be used with future

design thinking tools to come up with creative solutions for Universidad San Francisco de Quito. Unlike lengthy

spreadsheets and reports, mind mapping is accessible to students, professors, and administrators

alike.

The following page contains the mind map created to ask the what if portion of the question,

Design Thinking Tool: Story Telling

Challenge

My name is Alessio Putino and I am the Trainer-Training & Development for a group of  Engineering colleges in Andhra Pradesh, India. It is my responsibility to see that all  my Engineering students acquire a set of technical skills which are out of their  defined university curriculum. The main reason for this is because at the end of final  year of student course in Engineering, companies visit the colleges for placements  and recently these companies starting looking for additional technical skills in  students, apart from standard academic skills. Now, the challenge is to motivate  final year students to spend that extra hour of time in college for attending additional  technical training classes, as college time table for them is already hectic with their  regular academics and especially with final year project work. For the students, it is  very demotivating to stay in the college for an extra-hour regularly and then to go  home and practice those extra technical skills. It is even more difficult for those  students who commute college from different towns around, where the travel time  ranges from 40minutes to 90 minutes. The regular college hours are from 9am to  4pm and to accommodate this additional training session for one hour, we had to  extend the college timings till 5pm. As it turned out, the student attendance for these  training classes was lukewarm. So, we had a challenge to ensure healthy student  attendance for these classes and also to motivate them to go back home and spend  required time to practice these skills, which is in addition to their academic  homework.

Selection

I always use Story Telling to motivate students, to extract best out of them. Students  need inspiration to put those extra hours in their learning and practice. text:
Elevating social media content with a 'creative hack session’

Challenge and selection

I work at an agency, where I oversee a large team handling social media for a number of well- known brands. A large part of the work revolves around creating impactful, relevant content for  their respective target audiences. This involves my planning and creative teams working  together to come up with content themes and ideas for each brand, create a content calendar  (i.e. the copy and visuals that will be published on the various social platforms during that  month) and shared with clients for approval. The monthly calendars are based on key  communication pillars we align on with clients at the beginning of each year as they set the  tone for our content strategy. This process has been in place for years and it was working ﬁne until a few months ago; my  team started getting a lot of mixed feedback about content calendars for one brand, and  despite revisions clients were still unhappy with the content. My team started arranging calls to  go through the calendars and discussing them on a more regular basis, as well as pressing for  clearer feedback from clients as it was often vague and open to interpretation. There were  minor improvements, but it still didn’t solve the problem- clients were unhappy and they  started doubting our capabilities.

The challenge was to get everyone on the same page for social media content, so that we  deliver the product clients expect from us and regain our client's trust and satisfaction.

The tool I decided to use for to address this challenge was visualization. Clearly emails and  discussing the content was not working, so by using pictures and charts we can explore and  really understand our clients’ visions for their brand. It would also have clients get more  involved in the thinking process and feel like they have greater ownership over the direction of  content on their social media channels.

text: Design Thinking for Innovation  Assignment: Apply tools learned to a real life situation.        Example Reflection – Visualization     Challenge & Selection   We implemented SAP in our North America business unit, and after implementation we had the need to  support our finance team in three new post go-live activities: issue management, permanent training and  Change Management strategies. To tackle the issue, rather than using the standard solution (that is hiring  a SAP consulting firm to act on demand and in a case by case scenario), business made the decision of  adding a new staff position called “Finance Functional Expert Manager”.     But there are things that can be improved. Service and Finance team is divided into 7 different functional  areas (accounts receivable, accounts payable, product costing, etc.) spread across 3 different locations in  the US, supporting 52 users. Overall perception is little value added by the role, poor customer  satisfaction, service slowness, unclear communication, lack of clarity in expectations, and an inadequate  prioritization on issue management.     To improve this, customers – finance team – will be invited to participate on a visualization exercise to re- define the role IPE (ideal profile expected). From Design Thinking for Innovation, visualization is selected  as a tool given the number and different customer’s profiles, the diversity of activities performed, the  desire to involve customers as co-creators and to develop customer’s visualization skills (finance profiles  are commonly more comfortable with tools as data analysis, order, structure, etc.)      Application   First step will be to gather the whole team, in an informal environment and going through visualization  exercise. text:
Lex Communique – 2019

Client Counselling

▪ STRUCTURE OF COMPETITION

▪ There will be 2 rounds: preliminary round and final round.

▪ COMPOSITION OF TEAMS

▪ The team composition, for the competition, shall comprise of TWO participants.

▪ LANGUAGE

▪ The official language for Client Counselling shall be English.

▪ RULES OF COMPETITION:

▪ Preliminary Round shall be of 15 minutes each followed by Question & Answer session by the  judges, if any; not exceeding 10 minutes.

▪ The participating team with the highest scores in each Courtroom shall qualify for the Final  Round. Round shall be of 20 minutes each followed by Question & Answer session by the  judges, if any; not exceeding 10 minutes.

▪ Participants must take best endeavors to obtain information from Client for offering suitable  advice.

▪ Participants must take best efforts to offer a professional environment. For the same, usage of  office props can be brought by the Participants.

▪ Participants must provide options/ alternatives of their advice and explain the entire process  step wise as per the requirement of the Act.

▪ Participants must quote the chargeable fees to their client at the end of the counselling. (This  aspect shall be asked by our client on the spot to the participant)

▪ Usage of electronic gadgets shall not be allowed. Only books/ notes shall be permissible.

▪ Participants can discuss about the issue amongst themselves prior to offering any consultation  to the client.

▪ PARAMETERS OF EVALUATION:

▪ Clarity on concept and procedures

▪ Adherence to time

▪ Team coordination

▪ Professional etiquette, approach and environment offered to the client

▪ CLIENT BRIEFING AND ORIENTATION

▪ An orientation on basic information and Competition Rules for the clients shall be given in  advance of the date of Competition. But each client will be supplied with a packet containing the  consultation situation and a detailed confidential memorandum concerning the client's  background and concern

text:
Using Visualization Tool to teach co-create

the pedagogy vision of a Brazilian Business School

Challenge

I have worked since 2013 in the Teaching and Learning team of an important Business School  of Brazil.

In general, one of our challenges there is to align our pedagogy vision with our faculty.

For this, we have a blended program where our teachers study what is and how to apply our  pedagogy vision.

We finished the ninth class of the program last month.

Although we’re improving the course every class, we was already seeing differences between  the understandings of this central concept. So, this is our specific challenge: (i) to see how our  teachers understand our pedagogy vision and (ii) to show them what is the pedagogy vision  according our leaders.

That’s why in introduced the Visualization Tool, as I describe bellow.

Selection

I selected the Visualization Tool: using visual thinking to show and see ideas in instead of only  words.

According the video Visualization Tool, “It's  basically anything that takes us beyond just  using words or language alone. (…) When  we're talking and we're verbalizing things we  see things internally, but we may all be  understanding the words in a slightly  different way. The beauty of using  visualization is that we can tap into a single  picture”.

Application

Our blended course has two face-to-face classes. In the second face-to-face class, we used to  have an activity where teachers talk how they see the pedagogical vision. It was interesting,  but it was hard to discuss differences and similarities between all that ideas. That’s why we  decided to chance the activity: teachers don’t have only to say, but they have to draw the  concept.

So, we parted teachers in small groups and we followed some steps:

1) In small groups, teachers discuss what the  pedagogical vision of our institution is.

2) Each group draws this vision in a board.

3) Each group show and explain the vision to  other groups.

text:
Tool – Visualization

• Challenge: I was all set for a presentation on the affect of pollution on Global

Warming. I prepared a very good presentation mostly filled with hard statistics. As I  thought that people would be happy to get all the information in numbers as  numbers are easily comparable and they would also be able to digest things all the  information easily. Logical connectives can also be made much easier with numbers.  But at the end of the presentation I got very obvious question that were already  presented in the data in tabular format. So I understood that though I presented  every thing but my audience was able to digest very little of it.

• Selection: So I thought of selecting the visualization tool. With the help of this tool

we can present all the data in a more relevant visual format. That would make it  easier for people to digest. With a glance of any charts people can easily recognize  what’s happening. This is a very essential tool for any presenter.

• Application: So, what I did is to convert all the statistics to well presented charts.

And market important data points with different colors and arrows. I used proper  data labels and naming format and made the charts interactive. Then I prepared the  same presentation and presented in in front of similar kind of audience. I was  amazed to see the difference this time. People were easily able to grasp the entire  thing and they could easily remember the important data points. Even they came up  with very good questions that helped me to improve my presentation in the future.

• Insight: From the above experience, I came to understand that visualization is a

great way to make people remember things. A visually paired presentation helps  people to  easily understand the data and grasp things smoothly. A lot of data can be  easily incorporated in a chart and represented in a visual presentation. A non- technical person can also understand visualizations easily and quickly.

1. Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

A friend of me and I are currently working on a small startup idea in the field of professional  computer gaming. We´ll set up a transfer market information page for professional gamers  and teams. The challenge we´re working on is: how to get relevant and high quality data to  provide for the audience? Since professional gaming is not as mature as other sports, it´s not  that easy to get accurate data about gamers and teams.

2. Selection: In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected

I used the mind mapping tool to generate and cluster ideas and possibilities to gather the  necessary data.

3. Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge

The Mind Mapping was applied with a brainstorming session, a research / validation session  and an expert interview session. First of all we brainstormed as team, what kinds of gathering  methods are possible. We found four categories and clustered them on the map:  Crowdsourcing, manual input, Experts, and Data Providers. On the second step, we gathered  further information to every cluster on the internet and extended the mind map. We looked for  possible experts, looked for similar pages for other sports with crowdsourcing approaches and  how they´re doing it and so on. Finally we talked to relevant people in every cluster to finalize  the map. We talked for example to Data Providers, and Experts.

4. Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your  challenge

The value was very high and we gathered lots of great insights for our idea. Lots of the work  went directly into our pitch deck and we´ve selected expert input and crowdsourcing in  combination as the most valuable and cost effective methods. Especially the research and  interview data were very helpful.

Design thinking is a human centric ,interactive, solution -based, problem -solving framework.

Empathise

Prototype

Test

Reflection: Learning Launch – Onboarding guide

Challenge:

I am working for a relatively new consulting department within our company. When I joint the team, it  had a start up flair. This means the team existed for just two years and was a small group of people.  There was no visible structure of how to do things. It was more a learning by doing or a very sporadic  way to solve problems.

This being said, I had no clear instructions of organizational tasks (e.g. what access rights do I need) or  project tasks (e.g. where do I find our presentation guidelines) during my onboarding phase within this  team. The information either was given per forwarded emails piece by piece or verbally. For many topics  I had to ask for or research the information. Many times, I got stuck, had to wait or got frustrated while  searching for the right contact or answers.

Selection:

Due to this chaotic onboarding, I was seeing room for improvement in form of structure.

Besides investing a lot of my nerves, time and energy, my colleagues had experienced the same before.  My personal experience and the feedback of my colleagues was the data base for the What is phase.  Therefore, I decided to change the onboarding experience by creating a simple guide with steps, links  and contact information a new team member will need or even for colleagues to refer to later, if  needed. For example, when and how to request a corporate credit card and who to contact in case of  issues and the process behind it.

I have chosen the Learning Launch (“A small experiment that tests your new idea in the real  marketplace” Slides, Module 4) to test the created guide several times with colleagues and to adjust it  according to the feedbacks.

The fashion designers are locked to  the catalogues and magazines for style suggestions and may end up creating existent trends or left to  themselves when clients say make something nice that I don’t have.

text: Visualization tool – Sanne Aarts    Challenge As a strategic marketer working at an international bank in The Netherlands, I was  asked to create a vision on how money management will look like in the next 5 to 10 years.  Will we still have actual banks, or do we only have our smartphone on which we will manage  all our money? Or is it not even on a smartphone, but through virtual reality, were you talk to  you virtual assistant, who will tell you were to invest your money today and if you can budget  on your grocery shopping this week? And are banks the only ‘money management players’ in  the market by then, or will other industries also provide banking as a service? For example a  telco company, or a newly started fintech? A very difficult challenge, because basically, we  need a glass ball to see in the future! But we need to think about this, to be able to choose  what our position will be in that new world of money management.     Selection I chose to use the visualization tool, to help create a vision on the future of money  management. Why? Because this challenge calls for more than logic. I need a tool that can  give me insights in possibilities that aren’t yet possible now. Next to that, a vision is always  hard to put into words, in such a way, that all stakeholders interpret it the same way. And since  a strategic vision needs to be approved by multiple stakeholders, that is a real challenge. It is  easier to visualize it through a drawing, pictures, etc. That is why the visualization tool feels  like the right tool to use in this case.     Application For me it was important to make sure all possible knowledge on the money  management field would be present when working with the visualization tool. text:
1. Challenge : How do we make our customers adhere to the application of precautionary and

preventive measures against Covid 19 pandemic . During the recovery period , we noticed the  refusal of a small group of customers to apply precautionary measures such as have a negative  PCR for no more than 72 hours, wearing a mask , don’t have a fever and applying social distance  , which had a great impact on employees and thus to the interruption of service .

2. Selection : I will select the Learning Launch tool (module 4). It is a small experiment that tests

our new idea in the real work place . I will select this tool because it leaves an impact on the  customers that is difficult to forget and also it help customers to know impact of implementing  the precautionary measures against Covid 19 and why should they choose to .

3. Application : There will be two scenarios . The first scenario shows that X customer enters the

customer service center ignoring the precautionary measures and by doing that it helped spread  the virus among employees and the rest of the customers who applied the precautionary  measures , which led to the injury of some , disruption of work and an increase in expenses as a  result of the sterilization of the center .

4. Insight : By applying the selected tools we can convince the target group of the need to adhere

to the application of precautionary measures because everyone’s safety is safe . This theory  helped to discover the fault lines and work to correct them through updating and developing  the proposed idea to meet the challenge .

5.  Approach : Next time I will select different tool which is Story Telling ( Module 2 ) because this

tool has an amazing ability to persuade . Moreover , people like to listen to stories and learn the  lesson from the story told . Also , using different type of tools each time helps refine the idea  and creativity in the application .

gone through.

branches and then to sub branches. So I have selected mind mapping as a tool to my challenge

because I can remember it forever by creating a branch like structure in my mind and then

recollect and retrieve it whenever required.

Reflection "Mind Mapping"

Challenge & Selection

One of my favorite tools is Mind Mapping. Generally, I use it when I feel that  we have collected a lot of different data from different stakeholders:  customers, partners, participants and so on. For me, Mind Mapping is a sort  of the bridge between what is and what if  phase: we use it when we are  eager to begin generating ideas.     I’m a Product Designer for a consulting company so I use this tool often with  my clients while exploring different opportunities to innovate within their  company. I love this tool because it lets a lot of place to the imagination and  helps participants to understand the context of the customers lives instead  of seeing only business context.

Application

I start this exercise by laying all the data we have collected for everybody to  see it: for example, the good idea is to use a big light room. Visualize this  information helps to display the key components of what we have learned  during what is phase. Then, I invite different people and seat them at small

teams. I try to select very different people for this exercises. The only criteria is  to take curious and open-minded people, who are really interesting in what  you are doing.     Once everybody arrived, I distribute paper, stickers, markers, and  whiteboards to teams and explain the exercise. The important thing to do  here is to explain that they are here to help us to move forward and that  there are no good or wrong answers. Sometimes, I ask them to take off their  jackets and ties because it helps to put everyone on the same level and to be  more open-minded while working together.     Then, I ask everybody to make a tour of the room. Sometimes, I can give  them some additional explications about the information they can see. We believe that all kids are naturally creative and that every classroom should be filled with  creativity and wonder.

We want to see teachers unleash the creative potential in all of their students so that kids can  be makers, designers, artists, and engineers.

We know that school can be busy. Materials can be scarce. The creative process can seem  confusing, especially when you have a tight curriculum map. So creativity becomes a side  project, an enrichment activity you get to when you have time for it. But the thing is, there’s  never enough time.

We can do better.

We believe that creative thinking is as vital as math or reading or writing. There’s power in  problem-solving and experimenting and taking things from questions to ideas to authentic  products that you launch to the world. Something happens in students when they define  themselves as makers and inventors and creators.

That’s the power of design thinking. It provides a flexible framework for creative work. It’s  used in engineering, publishing, business, the humanities, in non-profit and community work.  And yes, it can be used in education! You can use it in every subject with every age group.  Although there are many versions of the design thinking model, we have developed the  LAUNCH Cycle as a student-friendly way to engage in design thinking.

We believe all students deserve the opportunity to be their best creative selves, both in and out  of school. We believe all kids are unique, authentic, and destined to be original.

Most importantly, we believe this is not an all-encompassing solution, but a start. We believe  our role is to empower kids to make an impact on the world around them and fully believe in  themselves.
